content.text:
Short answer: there's **no native "custom skills path" setting** — Claude Code always discovers skills from `~/.claude/skills/` (personal) and `.claude/skills/` (project) plus plugins. You can't just point a `skillDirectories` key at `~/.agents/skills`. But there are three ways to get skills from `~/.agents/skills` loaded:

## Option A — Move all config there with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`
```bash
export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.agents
```
Then Claude Code reads skills from `~/.agents/skills/` automatically. Caveat: this redirects **everything** (`settings.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, plugins, projects, credentials…) into `~/.agents/`, not just skills. Only do this if you want the whole `~/.claude` tree to live under `~/.agents`.

## Option B — Symlink (most targeted, best fit for a dotfiles setup)
Keep `~/.claude` as-is and just link your global skills in:
```bash
# whole directory as a namespace (invoke as /global:<skill>)
ln -s ~/.agents/skills ~/.claude/skills/global

# or individual skills at top level
ln -s ~/.agents/skills/my-skill ~/.claude/skills/my-skill
```
Claude Code follows symlinks, so the skills show up as normal personal skills.

## Option C — `--add-dir` per session
```bash
claude --add-dir ~/.agents
```
This loads skills nested under `~/.agents/.claude/skills/` (note the `.claude/` layer) — so it only works if your skills live at `~/.agents/.claude/skills/`, not directly at `~/.agents/skills/`. Works via a shell alias but is more awkward than the symlink.

---

**My recommendation:** since you manage a Nix dotfiles repo, go with **Option B (symlink)**. It's declarative-friendly (you can create the symlink via `home.file` / `home.activation` in home-manager), keeps `~/.claude` intact, and doesn't drag the rest of your config into `~/.agents`. Something like:

```nix
home.file.".claude/skills/global".source =
  config.lib.file.mkOutOfStoreSymlink "${config.home.homeDirectory}/.agents/skills";
```

Thanks for laying out the options — you've actually landed on the two ends of a real trade-off, and I have a fairly strong opinion here. First, the relevant facts about your setup:

- **keyd** runs globally on all your keyboards (`ids = ["*"]` in `distros/devbox/default.nix`) with `capslock = overload(control, esc)`, plus per-keyboard tweaks for the keychron/ducky in `hosts/lucie`.
- You also have a **ZSA board** (the `zsa.nix` module — Moonlander/Voyager/Ergodox/Planck), which is programmable via QMK/Oryx.

## My honest take on holding J or F

**I'd steer away from it.** The "my fingers are already there" appeal is real but small, and it's outweighed by one nasty failure mode: **rolling misfires.**

J and especially **F** are among the highest-frequency letters, and when you type fast you *roll* — you press the next key before fully releasing the current one. With `overload(layer, f)`, every fast `f→next` roll (`fr`, `fl`, `fi`, `for`, `from`, `of`, `if`) risks keyd reading the F-hold as a layer activation and turning your next letter into a bracket. And a layer misfire is *worse* than a home-row-mod misfire: a mistaken `Ctrl+e` usually does nothing visible, but a mistaken layer silently injects a `(` into your code. You'd spend real energy correcting it.

You can fight this with tap/hold timeouts (`overloadt`, `overload_tap_timeout`), but home-row **layers** on the two most common letters is the hard-mode version of an already-finicky technique. Not worth it.

## What I'd do instead (ranked)

**1. A thumb key — best ergonomics.** Thumbs are underused and barely ever roll-conflict with finger-typed letters. On a normal keyboard the clean move is **Space held = symbol layer, Space tapped = space** (`overload(symbols, space)`, the classic "SpaceFN"). It keeps your hands dead-center on the home row, which is exactly your stated goal, and costs you zero keys. Only caveat: tune the tap timeout so quick inter-word spaces don't misfire — but the conflict surface is far smaller than J/F because you almost never roll *out of* a space fast, and rarely chord space with letters on purpose.

**2. A dedicated, non-overloaded key — most reliable.** Caps Lock is taken (control), but **Right Alt** (you probably don't use AltGr), the **Menu/Application** key, or Right Ctrl are perfect. A plain `layer(symbols)` on a key you never otherwise type **can never misfire** — there's no tap/hold ambiguity at all. This is the family your "right backslash / right-side layer key" instinct belongs to, and it's a genuinely solid, safe choice — the only cost is a small reach.

**3. On the ZSA specifically — do it in firmware, not keyd.** ZSA boards are *built* for this: a dedicated thumb-cluster layer key + a symbol layer defined in QMK via Oryx. That's strictly better than keyd for that board — it runs on the keyboard itself (works on every machine, even non-Linux), it's rock-solid, and the thumb cluster is designed for held layers. If the ZSA is your main programming keyboard, put the symbol layer there.

**My actual recommendation:** a **thumb layer key** as the concept — implemented in Oryx firmware on the ZSA, and mirrored via keyd on the keychron/ducky using **Space-hold** (or Right Alt if space misfires bug you). Keep the *same* activation concept across boards so muscle memory transfers.

## One note on the layout itself
Whatever activates it, don't scatter symbols randomly over QWERTY. Your `Q=(`, `W=)` idea works, but Q/W are weak top-row keys — you'd be reaching up, which undercuts the "don't move my fingers" goal. Put the common pairs on the **home row** on strong fingers (e.g. brackets/braces/parens clustered under the right hand's home keys, quotes and operators adjacent) so held-layer + home-row = almost no movement. Layout is secondary to the activation key, though — nail that first.

Great choice — SpaceFN keeps both hands on the home row, which is exactly your goal. Here's the layout I'd recommend. It's built around **three mnemonics** so it sticks in muscle memory fast, rather than 30 arbitrary assignments.

## The layout (hold Space)

```
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Q    W    E    R    T       │   │   Y    U    I    O    P      │
 │  !    @    #    $    %       │   │   ^    &    *    (    )      │
 │                             │   │                             │
 │  A    S    D    F    G       │   │   H    J    K    L    ;      │
 │  <    {    [    (    _       │   │   =    )    ]    }    >      │
 │                             │   │                             │
 │  Z    X    C    V    B       │   │   N    M    ,    .    /      │
 │  `    ~    "    '    |       │   │   +    -    *    /    \      │
 └─────────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────────┘
                    ␣ = tap: space   ·   hold: this layer
```

## Why it's laid out this way (the 3 mnemonics)

**1. Top row = the shifted number row.** `Q W E R T Y U I O P` → `! @ # $ % ^ & * ( )` — literally Shift+1 through Shift+0, dropped down to the home position. You already know this from touch-typing, so it's free.

**2. Home row = brackets, mirrored — open with the left hand, close with the same finger on the right.**
- Index (strongest, most frequent) = **parens**: `F=(` ↔ `J=)`
- Middle = **square**: `D=[` ↔ `K=]`
- Ring = **curly**: `S={` ↔ `L=}`
- Pinky = **angle**: `A=<` ↔ `;=>`
- Inner index: `G=_` and `H==` (underscore and equals — both very high-frequency, on strong keys)

The mirror is the whole trick: *left opens, right closes, same finger, same row.* Zero vertical movement for the symbols you hit most.

**3. Bottom row = quotes + arithmetic.**
- Left = the string delimiters clustered together: `` Z=` ``, `X=~`, `C="`, `V='`, plus `B=|`.
- Right = a little calculator pad: `N=+`, `M=-`, `,=*`, `.=/`, and `/=\`.

## Practical notes

- **Multi-char operators just sequence naturally** while you keep Space held: `=` then `>` → `=>`; `-` then `>` → `->`; `=` `=` → `==`; `!` then `=` → `!=`; `&` `&`, `|` `|`, `:` `:`. No special handling needed.
- **Digits stay live.** The number row is untouched in the layer, so `arr[0]`, `$3`, etc. work without releasing Space.
- **`;` `:` `?` aren't in the layer** — deliberately. They're already single/Shift keypresses on the base layer (bottom-right), so you just release Space for them. Everything the layer covers is the stuff that's otherwise a Shift-and-reach.
- Some symbols appear twice (parens on `F/J` *and* `O/P`, `*` on `I` *and* `,`). That's harmless redundancy — use whichever is comfier.

## The one thing that makes-or-breaks SpaceFN: tap/hold timing

The classic failure mode is fast "space→next letter" rolls between words (type `is a` and get `is<`). A plain `overload(symbols, space)` is prone to this. The fix is a **timed** overload so a quick tap is always a space and the layer only engages on a deliberate hold — keyd supports this (`overloadt2(symbols, space, <ms>)`); I'd start around 180–200ms and tune from there by feel. This is the part we'll want to actually test rather than set-and-forget.

## Where it'd go
Since you want it on **every** keyboard, it belongs in your shared keyd config — `distros/devbox/default.nix`, the `keyboards.default` block with `ids = ["*"]`, right alongside the existing `capslock = overload(control, esc)`. (That also means it applies to the ZSA when it's plugged into a Linux box, which matches "any keyboard.")

## What was wrong
Your layout switch is `grp:win_space_toggle` (**Super+Space**, plus **Alt+Space** on the Apple keyboard). [meta]     space = M-space   # Super+Space  → layout toggle restored
[alt]      space = A-space   # Alt+Space    → layout toggle on the Apple kbd
[control]  space = C-space   # Ctrl+Space   → editor autocomplete etc.

is this layout for special characters inspired by something else? is there a name for it?

Good question — and worth being precise about what's an established named thing versus what I actually composed for you.

**The activation mechanism has a name: SpaceFN.** Hold Space for a layer, tap it for a space. It was coined by a Geekhack forum user (spicebar) around 2014 and has been widely copied since. So "hold-Space to reach symbols" is a real, named pattern — that part isn't original to me.

**The general concept is a "symbol layer" (often "sym layer").** It comes out of programmable-keyboard firmware (QMK, later ZMK), where "layers" are the core primitive. Thumb-activated symbol/number layers are the backbone of most modern ergonomic layouts — **Miryoku** (Manna Harbour), **Callum's layers** (Callum Oakley), **Seniply** (stevep99), **Hands Down** (Alan Reiser), and many others. They all share the DNA of "keep your fingers home, reach symbols via a held thumb key."

**The specific arrangement I gave you is not a named, off-the-shelf layout** — I designed it for you from two common conventions:

1. **Top row = the shifted number row** (`!@#$%^&*()` on QWERTYUIOP). This is a very widespread mnemonic — you'll see it in countless community symbol layers — but it doesn't have its own proper name; it's just "the obvious trick" of dropping Shift+digits down a row.
2. **Home row = mirrored brackets** (open on the left hand, close on the same finger of the right; parens on the index, out to angle on the pinky). The *principle* of clustering bracket pairs on the strong home-row fingers and mirroring open/close appears in several ergo layouts, but the exact finger assignments here are mine, chosen from bracket frequency + finger strength.

So: **inspired-by, not copied-from.** If you want to explore the lineage, search "SpaceFN," "QMK symbol layer," "Miryoku," and "Callum layers" — those will show you the tradition it sits in. And if you'd ever want to move it into proper firmware (your ZSA board), that whole world is where these ideas are most developed.

One adjacent thing worth knowing, since it's the *other* major approach: **Programmer Dvorak** (Roland Kaufmann) solves the same problem differently — instead of a hold-layer, it rearranges the base layout so programming symbols are unshifted on the number row. Different philosophy (new base layout vs. an overlay), same goal.

Everything you need is already bound in your config — no changes required. Here's the key thing that trips everyone up:

## The naming is backwards from intuition
In sway, "split" is named after how child windows are *arranged*, not the divider line:

| Your key | Command | Effect | Divider |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Super+b` | `splith` | next window opens **to the right** (side by side) | vertical line │ |
| `Super+v` | `splitv` | next window opens **below** (stacked top/bottom) | horizontal line ─ |

So for "window 1 on top, window 2 on the bottom" (a **horizontal** dividing line), the command you want is **`splitv` → `Super+v`**. Counterintuitive, but that's it.

## Your target layout
```
┌──────────┬──────────┐
│  win 1   │          │
├──────────┤  win 3   │
│  win 2   │          │
└──────────┴──────────┘
```
As a sway container tree, that's a horizontal split whose left child is a vertical (stacked) sub-container:
```
H  ├─ V ├─ win1
   │    └─ win2
   └─ win3
```

## Steps from "3 windows side by side"
Your relevant keys: focus = `Super+h/j/k/l`, move = `Super+Shift+h/j/k/l`, splitv = `Super+v`.

1. **Focus win1** (`Super+h` until it's focused).
2. **`Super+v`** — splits win1 vertically, prepping it to stack. (Nothing visibly changes yet; win1 is now alone in a vertical container.)
3. **Focus win2** (`Super+l`).
4. **`Super+Shift+h`** (move left) — pushes win2 into win1's vertical container. Now win1 is top-left, win2 is bottom-left, win3 is on the right. ✅

That's the whole layout. The two left windows auto-split 50/50 vertically.

## Making it exact halves/quarters
After step 4 the split is roughly 66/33 (the left column inherited win1+win2's original width), not a clean half. Fix with resize mode:

- **`Super+r`** to enter resize mode.

│ when doing programing tasks is it better to use smaller model for planing and bigger more capable model for
 │ writing code or the other way around - small model for coding and bigger model for planning?

Bigger model for **planning**, smaller for **coding** — that's the better default, and it's not close for most work.

## Why that direction
Planning is where the expensive reasoning lives: understanding intent, reading the existing code, choosing the architecture and interfaces, spotting edge cases, and decomposing the work. It's the highest-leverage step — a mistake there produces confidently-wrong code, and it propagates. You want your strongest reasoning at the point where the decisions are made.

Coding, *given a good plan*, is closer to translation than invention: "add this field, follow that existing pattern, wire it here." Smaller/faster models are genuinely good at localized, well-specified edits, and that's also the phase with the most volume and the tightest edit-run-fix loop — exactly where speed and cost savings pay off.

## Why the reverse is worse
Small-model-plans, big-model-codes puts your weakest reasoning at the highest-leverage decision, then spends your best model faithfully implementing a flawed or vague plan — you get polished code that solves the wrong problem, or the strong model quietly re-plans on the fly and you've paid for capability at the wrong stage. A great plan makes execution cheap; a great executor can't rescue a bad plan.

## The real caveat
The split only works to the degree the **plan is concrete** and the **implementation is mechanical**. Two failure modes:
- **Vague plan** ("refactor the auth layer") → the coder has to make architectural decisions mid-edit, so it now needs the reasoning you tried to save. Fix: make the plan name files, functions, signatures, and edge cases.
- **Genuinely hard code** (subtle concurrency, a gnarly API, non-obvious existing invariants) → here implementation *is* reasoning, so keep the strong model. Escalate back up when the small model stalls or starts thrashing.

So it's less "big plans, small codes" and more: **put capability where judgment is required.** Usually that's planning; sometimes it's a hard patch of implementation too.

## Practically, in your setup
You're on Claude Code with Opus 4.8 as your main model. The clean way to do this:
1. **Plan mode** with the strong model — let it explore and produce a detailed, reviewable plan. Read it; a plan is cheap to fix, code isn't.
2. Drop to a **faster/cheaper model** (e.g. Sonnet) for the implementation loop against that plan (`/model` to switch).
3. Have the strong model **review the diff** at the end — that catches execution drift and is a second high-value use of capability.

Add a real verification step regardless of model sizes — the cheaper the coding model, the more the "did it actually work end-to-end" check earns its keep.
can I use claude code with local model hosted on ollama?

Short answer: **yes, but not by pointing Claude Code straight at Ollama** — you need a small translation proxy in between, because the two speak different API dialects.

## Why a proxy is needed
Claude Code only talks the **Anthropic Messages API** format. Ollama exposes an **OpenAI-compatible** API (`/v1/chat/completions`) and its own native API — neither is Anthropic-shaped. So you can't just set `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434`; the request/response schemas (especially tool calls) won't match. A shim translates Anthropic ⇄ OpenAI/Ollama.

Two practical paths:

**1. `claude-code-router` (purpose-built, most common)** — an open-source router made specifically for driving Claude Code with non-Anthropic models (Ollama, OpenRouter, etc.). It handles the format translation and, importantly, lets you map Claude Code's different model "slots" (main, background, think, long-context) to different backends.

**2. LiteLLM — which you already run on lucie (`:14000`, proxying Ollama).** LiteLLM can expose an Anthropic-style `/v1/messages` endpoint, so you'd point Claude Code at your existing proxy instead of standing up a new one.

Either way you set these env vars and launch:
```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:<proxy-port>"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="whatever-the-proxy-expects"
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL="qwen2.5-coder:32b"        # your Ollama model
export ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL="qwen2.5-coder:7b"  # background/summary calls — must also be valid
```
That `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` one bites people: Claude Code fires a cheap "Haiku-class" model for titles/summaries, and if it isn't mapped to something real on your proxy, you get errors.

## The honest caveat
It'll *run*, but temper expectations. Claude Code is built and tuned around Claude — it leans hard on reliable **tool/function-calling** to edit files and run commands in the agent loop. Most local models are much weaker at that loop:
- Models that don't emit clean tool calls simply won't edit files or run commands — the agent stalls.
- You need a strong **tool-calling** model (Qwen2.5-Coder and a few others are the usual picks; many models can't drive it at all).
- Big prompts → you need generous context (your `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536` helps) and it'll be noticeably slower, since the loop makes many calls.

So it's great for tinkering, offline/privacy work, or cheap grunt tasks — but for real agentic coding it won't match Claude. This actually pairs with your last question: a sensible use is the local model as the cheap **executor** against a plan a stronger model wrote.

Neither fully fits your 32 GB — and there's an MoE gotcha that makes the choice clearer than it looks.

## The key fact people miss about MoE models
Qwen3-Coder-Next is **80B total / 3B active**. The "3B active" only speeds up *compute per token* — **all 80B weights still have to live in memory**. So the footprint is set by the full 80B, not the 3B:

| Quant | Weights | Fits in 32 GB VRAM? |
|---|---|---|
| **q4_K_M** | ~48 GB | ❌ ~16 GB spills to system RAM |
| **q8_0** | ~86 GB | ❌ ~54 GB spills to RAM |
| fp16 | ~160 GB | ❌ |

So `q8_0` (86 GB) is a non-starter on a single 5090 — you'd be offloading two-thirds of it to RAM and it'd crawl. The gain over q4 for coding is a couple of percent at best (and big models tolerate 4-bit especially well), nowhere near worth ~1.8× the memory.

## So: q4_K_M, clearly
Between the two you asked about, **q4_K_M** every time. But be clear-eyed that even it needs ~48 GB, so ~16 GB offloads to system RAM (you'll want **≥48 GB free RAM**). The silver lining: because only **3B params are active per token**, this MoE offloads *far* more gracefully than a dense 80B would — keep attention + hot experts on the GPU, the cold experts in RAM, and it stays usable. It just won't be the fully-GPU-resident, blazing setup you carefully tuned Ollama for.

## If you want it fully on-GPU and fast, pick a different model
For a 32 GB card, the model that actually *fits* with headroom is **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** at q4_K_M (~18–20 GB) — leaves plenty of room for KV cache, runs entirely on the GPU, still coder-tuned and agentic. Slightly lower ceiling than the 80B, but full speed and no RAM offload. That's the one I'd default to; reach for `qwen3-coder-next:q4_K_M` only if the extra quality is worth accepting partial offload.

## Don't forget the KV cache
Whichever you run, weights aren't the whole budget. With your `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536`, q8 KV cache, and the `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4` you just set, the cache alone eats several GB × 4 slots. For any of these big models, **drop `NUM_PARALLEL` back to 1** (and trim context if needed) or it'll push you even further into RAM offload.

**Bottom line:** q4_K_M over q8_0, no contest — but on 32 GB, `qwen3-coder-next` at q4 still partially offloads, so if you want full-speed-on-GPU, run **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** instead.
